newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yamaichi Securities heads to quit - papers.
newsitem.headline: Yamaichi Securities heads to quit - papers.

text.p: The heads of embattled Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd will resign en masse as the firm awaits possible stiff penalties for suspected illegal deals with an alleged corporate racketeer, Japanese media on Saturday quoted company sources as saying.

Financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun quoted Yamaichi officials as saying the scandal-plagued firm would ask chairman Tsugio Yukihira and president Atsuo Miki and other top officials to stand down to take responsibility for alleged illegal payoffs from Ryuichi Koike.
A company spokesman was not available for comment.
Tokyo prosecutors allege the brokerage gave Koike 79 million yen ($686,000) in violation of the Commercial Code and Securities and Exchange Law to reimburse him for securities trading losses.
Yamaichi allegedly made the payments in 1995 to obtain Koike's help in ensuring that its annual shareholders' meeting went smoothly, domestic media reported.

Yamaichi senior managing director Shoji Saotome will replace Yukihira as chairman, while senior managing director Shohei Nozawa will succeed Miki as president, Japanese media quoted company sources as saying.

The reports came as Yamaichi awaited possible crippling punishment after the Finance Ministry on July 30 imposed the harshest ever penalties imposed in Japan for violations of securities or banking laws on giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd for their involvement in the payoff scandal.

The scandal, which is unfolding just as Japan begins its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in its stodgy financial sector, has aroused harsh criticism of a lack of transparency amongst Japan's financial institutions.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, under pressure to crack down after years of lax supervision of financial institutions, has said stern steps could be expected against Yamaichi once the probe was completed.

Yamaichi would likely suffer more than securities giant Nomura should the smaller firm be hit with similar penalties as it lacks an equity cushion and is ill-prepared to adapt to deregulation measures, analysts said.

Prosecutors are also conducting investigations into the other two of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd, in connection with the affair, Japanese media reported.
"Sokaiya" racketeers buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices.
The corporate raiders are also employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
